subject: Copywriting
title: Prebunking: Inoculating Against Lies
description: A micro-lesson that makes Prebunking: Inoculating Against Lies usable.

hook.text: Prebunking exposes people to weakened propaganda before they encounter the real thing.

buildup.text: Google's Jigsaw unit created short videos showing manipulation techniques.

discovery.text: Inoculation theory: expose people to a weak version of an argument, and they develop antibodies against the real thing.

twist.text: Prebunking works better than debunking. Once someone believes a lie, correcting it often strengthens the belief.

climax.text: Governments including the UK and EU now invest in prebunking campaigns.

punchline.text: Expose the trick first, and the propaganda fails. Prebunking works 21% better.

quiz.question: How much better at spotting fake news were viewers of Google's prebunking videos?

details.summary: Prebunking is the practice of exposing people to weakened forms of misinformation before they encounter the real thing — like a vaccine for the mind. Research shows that warning people about manipulation techniques in advance makes them significantly more resistant to propaganda.
details.whyItMatters: Debunking misinformation after the fact is difficult because first impressions stick. Prebunking works proactively, building resistance before exposure, making it one of the most effective tools against modern propaganda.
takeaways: Prebunking exposes people to weakened misinformation to build resistance
It works like inoculation: small doses of the threat build immunity
Prebunking is more effective than debunking after the fact

faq.question: How does prebunking work?
faq.answer: By showing people examples of manipulation techniques — emotional language, false experts, conspiracy logic — in a safe context before they encounter real propaganda. This forewarning activates critical thinking so that when real misinformation appears, the brain recognizes the pattern.

faq.question: Is there scientific evidence that prebunking works?
faq.answer: Yes. Studies at Cambridge University and Google's Jigsaw team have shown that short prebunking videos reduce susceptibility to misinformation by up to 30%. The effect works across political ideologies and lasts for weeks after exposure.
